title: Tara's mantra
hookLine: om tare tuttare ture soha, the mantra of Tara

lines: A LONG OPENING, THREE STEPS, A LANDING.
cards: Om tare tuttare ture soha. Said slowly, it has a shape: a long opening, three words that tumble down like steps, then a soft landing. Said fast, under the breath, it can sound like water running over stones.
People in Tibetan Buddhist communities say it in kitchens and on buses, over sick children and before long journeys, often counting on a string of beads.
You first met Tara back in year one, one foot already stepping down. Today, the sound that calls her.

teach.b: First, who Tara is: a female bodhisattva, an awakened being who stays to help. One story says she was born from the tears of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, as he wept over the suffering of the world.
Another tells of a princess who was told to pray to be reborn as a man, and instead vowed to wake up, and keep helping, as a woman. Second, the mantra.
It's Sanskrit, and it plays on her own name, often explained as she who carries across, or she who saves.

Tare, tuttare, ture: the name turned three ways, like calling someone, then calling again more urgently. Om opens it, and soha, the Tibetan way of saying the Sanskrit svaha, closes it, as it closes many mantras.
Third, quickness. Tibetan devotion calls Tara swift.

In her green form she's seated, left leg drawn in for meditation, right foot stepping down off her lotus. Teachers say that foot shows she's ready to rise the moment she's called. That's your line: she comes quickly.

teach.h: IN FEAR, FOR OTHERS, EVERY DAY.
teach.b: Some recite it in danger or fear, some for someone else's sake, some simply as a daily practice, letting the sound steady the mind.
Tradition holds that the mantra is a way to meet her compassion.

how: Tibetan Buddhists recite Tara's mantra, om tare tuttare ture soha, often on a mala, in daily practice, in times of fear or danger, and on behalf of others.

o: a lullaby Tibetan parents sing to children
a Sanskrit blessing said only at funerals
a chant that calls Tara's name three ways

p: a female bodhisattva known as swift
the Tibetan way of saying svaha

s: it's Sanskrit; only soha is the Tibetan way of saying svaha.
one story says Tara was born from Avalokiteshvara's tears
as he wept over the suffering of the world.
green Tara is shown with both legs folded in meditation
her right foot steps down off her lotus, ready to rise.

games.q: you're the princess in the old story. you've vowed to wake up, and you're told to pray to be reborn as a man first. what do you do?
o: agree, and pray to be reborn as a man.
vow to wake up and keep helping as a woman.
games.why: in the story told about Tara, she refuses and vows to awaken, and keep helping, as a woman.

practice: If you wish, say it seven times, aloud or under your breath, slowly, counting on your fingers: om tare tuttare ture soha.

If someone you know is frightened or struggling, you can hold them in mind while you chant; if chanting isn't yours, hear the rhythm in your head, or count seven slow breaths instead. Then rest in the quiet after the last soha.

wordCard.voice: Tara's mantra. Om tare tuttare ture soha: her name, called three ways, for the bodhisattva known as swift. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: she comes quickly. One foot already stepping down off the lotus. I'll be here tomorrow.
